cim: Lawyers offer recommendations on proposed AI ethics opinion

cim_eredeti: Lawyers offer recommendations on proposed AI ethics opinion
szoveg_eredeti:
A Florida Bar committee’s proposed advisory opinion regarding artificial intelligence is generating suggestions from a handful of attorneys, most of whom are eager for more guidance.

The Special Committee on Artificial Intelligence Tools and Resources requested an advisory opinion earlier this year, and the Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics posted a public notice October 15.

Although a draft is not yet available, the notice advised that it may cover lawyers’ use of agentic AI tools; the use of artificial intelligence tools to record, transcribe, and summarize communications; guidance to clients regarding their use of artificial intelligence tools; and updates to guidance provided in Florida Ethics Opinion 24-1.

Gainesville lawyer Nathan Nevins, one of eight attorneys who submitted comments as of November 3, is the only commenter opposed to most lawyers’ use of the technology. A partner with Sunshine State Probate, Nevins is board certified in wills, trusts and estates. He was admitted to the Bar in 2013.

AI use by attorneys for anything other than legal research should be “wholly banned,” Nevins recommends, adding that even then, the research results should be “double checked by each attorney.”

Attorneys are forwarding AI-generated proposals to their opponents and getting back AI-generated responses or counter proposals, Nevins warns.

“We literally have scenarios now where we have AI negotiating contracts with other AI,” Nevins wrote. “This is what we want the legal profession to turn into?”

Ryan Enage, a civil trial lawyer with Lloyd & McDaniel and a Florida Bar member since 2022, notes that the Florida Supreme Court this summer amended Florida Rule of General Practice and Judicial Administration 2.515(d)(2)(Representation by Signer). The amendments state that by filing, the signer of a document represents that “the legal authorities identified exist and are accurately cited.”

The Supreme Court order noted that while AI tools can be helpful, they also can generate content that appears plausible but is in fact inaccurate, including fabricated or “hallucinated” authorities, Enage notes. He also notes that Florida judges in 2000 recommended that pleadings prepared by an attorney and filed on behalf of a pro-se litigant indicate “Prepared with the Assistance of Counsel.”

He recommends that “pleadings or other papers in which artificial intelligence was used in their preparation and filed with the court, both prepared by attorneys and prepared by unrepresented parties…indicate ‘Prepared with Assistance of Artificial Intelligence.’”

Hialeah attorney Arianna Mendez, a Florida Bar member since 2020, says her practice focuses mostly on commercial litigation, business transactions, and real estate disputes.

“In my practice, clients have brought me AI-generated legal advice and have shared sensitive information with AI tools,” Mendez writes. “These experiences have raised concerns for me about the discovery implications of clients’ independent use of AI: what records they are creating, what information they are disclosing, and what may need to be preserved.”

Clients may be mistakenly viewing their use of AI as a “private exchange,” she writes.

“I would welcome guidance on how lawyers should counsel clients about these risks, including potential requests for prompts, uploaded materials, and responses.”

Jason K. Castro, an attorney with Golden Gate Legal Center, has been a Florida Bar member since 2015.

Generative and agentic AI tools enable lawyers to “research, prepare, compare, and revise legal documents at a pace that was previously unimaginable,” Castro observes.

The increased pace, Castro warns, also creates “new opportunities” for human error.

Castro asks that Bar regulators not confuse “revision fatigue” and “version-control risks” with “intentional misconduct or reckless disregard” of an attorney’s professional obligations.

“The circumstances surrounding the error, the reasonableness of the attorney's precautions, and the attorney's response upon discovery should inform any assessment under the applicable Rules Regulating The Florida Bar,” Castro writes.

Florida Bar Ethics Counsel Jonathan Grabb says the Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics will review the comments and the proposed advisory opinion at a December 10 meeting.

The committee could proceed with the draft as proposed, modify it, withdraw it from consideration, or take other action, such as forming a subcommittee, Grabb says.

Once a draft is proposed, it will be noticed in the News prior to consideration by the Board of Governors.

(Editor’s Note: Lawyers and law firms should conduct their own analysis and consider all relevant facts, professional obligations, and applicable rules before adopting any new technology. Florida Ethics Opinion 24-1 addresses many of the ethics issues related to using AI.)
